title: What must a 3D scene representation know before a robot can act?
dek: Scene perception turns observations into objects, relations, and usable parts. This guide follows the shift from geometric labels to language-queryable and action-relevant scene structure.
intro: A kitchen scan can be dense, colorful, and still leave a robot unsure what to do. It has to tell the counter from the cabinet, isolate one refrigerator from the next appliance, notice that a thin bar is a handle, and work out what moves when that handle is pulled. Those are different inferences, layered on the same geometry.

The literature has grown around those layers. Some methods learn features anchored in local 3D neighborhoods. Others group points into objects, attach free-form language to those objects, or identify the parts that invite a particular action. Functional and articulation work brings the question closest to robotics: which surface can be used, and what state change should follow?

There is no single scene representation that is best at all of this. A language feature may retrieve a 'drawer' in a room; a manipulation system also needs the drawer's front face, a possible handle, and room for motion. We move from geometric labels to object identity, language grounding, and action-relevant structure with that distinction in view.

sections.heading: Begin with the unit of prediction
paragraphs: A semantic map labels each observation with a class such as wall, cabinet, or chair. An instance map separates two cabinets of the same class. Panoptic prediction keeps both decisions. This distinction matters in a cluttered room: a planner cannot choose the left cabinet if both cabinets collapse into one semantic region.

Point-set backbones decide which neighbors get to inform a prediction. PointNet reads a whole set, while PointNet++ introduces a hierarchy of local neighborhoods [cite:pointnet] [cite:pointnet-plus-plus]. PTv3 and Volt make later choices about how sparse room-scale evidence is organized before a task head turns it into labels or masks [cite:ptv3] [cite:volume-transformer].

At room scale, this is also a compute decision. Fine point-level processing retains thin handles and boundaries but can be costly over a dense scan. Superpoint, sparse, and octree abstractions make wider context cheaper but can merge nearby surfaces or erase small functional elements [cite:superpoint-graph] [cite:superpoint-transformer] [cite:octformer]. Before interpreting a result, ask whether the model saw an isolated object, a fused room scan, or a temporal stream; the spatial support determines what ambiguity it can resolve.

sections.heading: From classes to objects
paragraphs: Instance segmentation adds a grouping problem. Bottom-up systems can aggregate nearby points; PointGroup, HAIS, and SoftGroup make this family concrete [cite:pointgroup] [cite:hais] [cite:softgroup]. Query-based systems can predict masks directly. Mask3D and OneFormer3D make a useful contrast because the latter explicitly brings semantic, instance, and panoptic predictions into one transformer formulation [cite:mask3d] [cite:oneformer3d].

A clean mask is not yet a physical object model. It may describe only what was visible, merge two adjacent objects, or say nothing about the geometry that produced it. In a real kitchen, that difference is practical: a planner that cannot separate the left cabinet from the right one cannot choose a door to open.

sections.heading: Make the scene queryable in language
paragraphs: Fixed taxonomies make it difficult to ask for an unfamiliar object or a descriptive concept. Open-vocabulary systems instead associate visual-language features with 3D regions. OpenScene transfers such features into 3D, while OpenMask3D and Open3DIS operate around instance masks or proposals [cite:openscene] [cite:openmask3d] [cite:open3dis]. ConceptFusion broadens the query interface beyond text to other modalities [cite:conceptfusion].

Language does not replace geometry. 'The cabinet left of the oven' names an instance and a spatial relation, not merely a compatible text embedding. ConceptGraphs makes that connection explicit by building an open-vocabulary scene graph from RGB-D observations for later queries and planning [cite:conceptgraphs]. This is why a fixed-class score is only part of the story for open-world grounding.

sections.heading: Recognize the parts that change the task
paragraphs: Interaction adds a finer target than an object category. Opening a refrigerator calls for a door or handle, a joint type, an axis or motion direction, and clearance for the robot. GAPartNet frames actionable parts across categories; OPD and OPDMulti estimate openable parts and motion parameters from one image, including multi-object views [cite:gapartnet] [cite:opd] [cite:opdmulti]. Earlier category-level work on articulated pose and tracking makes the state-estimation problem explicit [cite:ancsh] [cite:captra].

Scene-scale functionality is harder because parts are small, connected to cluttered furniture, and embedded in a room. SceneFun3D links functional-element masks, affordances, task descriptions, and interaction motions. Articulate3D records parts, connectivity, articulation, and executable scene structure [cite:scenefun3d] [cite:articulate3d]. These are related but not interchangeable outputs: a function label, a movable-part mask, and a simulator-ready relation answer different questions. A single-view motion estimate can remain ambiguous even when the visible part boundary is accurate.

sections.heading: Use temporal and geometric evidence to resolve state
paragraphs: A room scan is usually the result of a sequence, even when it is delivered as one fused point cloud. That sequence contains information that a single view does not: a handle may appear only from an oblique angle, a movable part may be revealed after another object shifts, and repeated observations can distinguish sensor noise from a persistent edge. CAPTRA addresses category-level articulated pose tracking from point clouds, making temporal state rather than one-shot recognition the central output [cite:captra].

Geometric-semantic coupling is another route to interaction understanding. Segment–Snap explicitly connects geometry and semantics in 3D scenes [cite:segment-snap]. The broader lesson is that semantic labels should not float independently of the coordinate frame, observed surfaces, and candidate contacts that support them. A robot that receives a label for ‘drawer’ but not the local geometry around its front face cannot readily choose a grasp pose or tell whether opening is blocked.

More views help, but they do not settle every case. A seam in a static scan may not be a joint; motion can reveal movement without revealing the exact constraint behind it. Good systems keep that uncertainty visible and make room for another view or a careful contact. That is where passive scene understanding becomes embodied perception.

sections.heading: Choose an output for the next decision
paragraphs: Segmentation tells us whether a model recognizes the annotated target. It does not show that a robot can grasp, open, or recover after contact. Retrieval may only need language features; mapping needs identities that survive a revisit; manipulation needs a local surface, a candidate motion, and often a confidence estimate.

For that reason, read every result with its sensing setup and intended use in mind: point cloud, RGB-D, images, or video; visible region or completed structure; semantic label or action hypothesis. The scene model needed by a long-running agent must also survive change—a door opens, an object moves, and a later view resolves an earlier mistake.

callout.title: Evaluation boundary
callout.text: A benchmark validates its annotated target. It does not, by itself, validate an executable twin or a manipulation policy.

takeaway: A useful 3D scene representation is layered: geometry supports regions, regions support instances, language makes them queryable, and functional structure makes selected regions actionable. The right layer is defined by the decision that follows it.
